lines: Let the [[Axiom:Axiom of Choice|Axiom of Choice]] be accepted.
Let $\powerset S$ be the [[Definition:Power Set|power set]] of $S$.
By the [[Axiom:Axiom of Choice|Axiom of Choice]], there is a [[Definition:Choice Function|choice function]] $c$ defined on $\powerset S \setminus \set \O$.
We will use $c$ and the [[Principle of Transfinite Induction]] to define a [[Definition:Bijection|bijection]] between $S$ and some [[Definition:Ordinal|ordinal]].

Intuitively, we start by pairing $\map c S$ with $0$, and then keep extending the [[Definition:Bijection|bijection]] by pairing $\map c {S \setminus X}$ with $\alpha$, where $X$ is the set of elements already dealt with.
Suppose $s_\beta$ has been defined for all $\beta < \alpha$.
The process eventually stops, else we have defined bijections between subsets of $S$ and arbitrarily large ordinals.

Now, we can impose a [[Definition:Well-Ordering|well-ordering]] on $S$ by embedding it via $s_\alpha \to \alpha$ into the ordinal $\beta = \ds {\bigcup_{s_\alpha \mathop \in S} \alpha}$ and using the [[Definition:Well-Ordering|well-ordering]] of $\beta$.
